standard: GDD rework v2 · 80+ researched scenarios · scorecard-passed
note: Building healthy adult relationships; recognising & leaving unhealthy ones; breakups (UNESCO 1.2, 5.3, 4.1, 5.6). New v2 build, the relationship heart of College. Good relationships are built, not found. Five modes: what healthy looks like, fight right (the Four Horsemen and repair), red flags grown up (coercive control, jealousy-as-love, isolation, gaslighting; UN&RE), leaving safely & breakups, tools/help. Abuse-aware: coercive control named clearly, leaving framed as valid and brave and never the target's fault, exit-safety handled with care (abuse can escalate at leaving). Breakup content is wellbeing-safe (healthy coping, no-contact, rebuilding; links g39 Bounce and g49 Mind & Belonging); non-graphic. Even-handed across genders; routes disclosures to help. Builds on g24 (Green Light/Red Light), g31 (Mutual), g09 (Friend or Frenemy); between g45 and g47; on-ramp to Chapter 7. India: relationships under family scrutiny, 'caring vs controlling' romanticised in culture; helplines 181, 1091, 112.

evidenceBase: Healthy relationships are built skills, not luck: mutual respect, trust, equality, honest communication, independence (your own friends and identity), support and repair after conflict. Conflict itself is normal; what matters is how you handle it. Gottman's research identifies four damaging patterns, criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling, that predict relationship breakdown with high accuracy, with contempt (sarcasm, name-calling, eye-rolling) the single most corrosive; the antidotes are gentle 'I' statements, appreciation and respect, taking responsibility, and self-soothing breaks then returning to repair (UNESCO ITGSE KC1; Gottman; One Love healthy-relationship signs)

Coercive control is not love: monitoring location, demanding passwords or dictating clothing and finances 'for transparency' is control (healthy transparency is voluntary), isolation from friends and family makes a person dependent and easier to control, and gaslighting ('you're too sensitive', 'that never happened') makes them doubt their own reality. Jealousy and possessiveness are about control, not romance, and 'they're just protective' is how control gets romanticised; love expands your world while control shrinks it (UNESCO KC4; coercive-control and toxic-relationship research)

Leaving an unhealthy or unsafe relationship is valid and brave and never the target's fault; because abuse can escalate around the time of leaving, exit-safety matters: tell someone, have a safe place and key documents, and lean on support and helplines. Breakups are real grief and survivable: no-contact aids healing, healthy coping (not numbing or self-harm) and rebuilding your own life and identity carry you through, and it is not a verdict on your worth. Even-handed across genders; India helplines 181, 1091, 112 (UNESCO KC4; survivor-safety and breakup-wellbeing practice)

scenarios.hook: Sort: a marker of a healthy relationship, or not?

items.text: You can be honest without fear
You each keep your own friends
One person calls all the shots

scenarios.relearn: Honesty without fear and keeping your own friends is healthy; eggshells and one-sided control aren't.

scenarios.hook: Sam: good relationships are built, with skills, not just found by luck. Sit right with you?
scenarios.affirm: Seeing love as something you build, with real skills, is what makes lasting ones possible.
scenarios.relearn: Healthy relationships are built with skills, not found by luck.

scenarios.hook: Your partner wants you to drop a hobby to spend all your time together.

options.text: Keep your own life; a healthy bond has space in it
options.consequence: You protect your independence.

options.text: Give it up to prove your love
options.consequence: Healthy love keeps your own life and space; you don't have to give yourself up.

scenarios.debrief: Independence, your own friends, hobbies and identity, is a marker of a healthy relationship.
scenarios.relearn: Healthy love keeps your own friends, hobbies and identity.

scenarios.hook: Sort: builds trust, or erodes it?
scenarios.relearn: Keeping your word and being reliable builds trust; snooping and testing erode it.

scenarios.hook: You and your partner disagree on something that matters to you both.

options.text: Talk it through as equals and find a middle
options.consequence: You practise equality and communication.

options.text: Whoever's louder or sulks longest wins
options.consequence: Healthy couples decide as equals; loudest or sulkiest 'winning' isn't it.

scenarios.debrief: Equality, deciding together rather than one person dominating, is a core healthy marker.
scenarios.relearn: Healthy couples decide as equals, not by who dominates.

scenarios.hook: Sort: healthy support, or smothering?

items.text: Needing to know their every move
Being there in a hard week

scenarios.relearn: Cheering their goals and being there is support; tracking them and resenting others is smothering.

scenarios.hook: You want your partner to feel genuinely valued.
scenarios.relearn: Showing genuine appreciation keeps a relationship healthy.
scenarios.setup: Show appreciation, the antidote to contempt. Say:

yourLine.text: "I really appreciate you, and I'm grateful you're in my life."
Point out their flaws to keep them humble

scenarios.hook: Things are good, and you want to keep them that way.

options.text: Keep communicating, appreciating and repairing
options.consequence: You maintain the relationship like the skill it is.

options.text: Coast and assume it'll stay good on its own
options.consequence: Healthy relationships are maintained with ongoing care; coasting lets them drift.

scenarios.debrief: Even good relationships are kept healthy with ongoing communication and appreciation.
scenarios.relearn: Keep a good relationship healthy with ongoing care, not coasting.

scenarios.hook: Spot the healthy sign.

scene.text: You feel free to be yourself
You hide parts of your life to keep peace

scenarios.why: Feeling free to be yourself and owning mistakes is healthy; hiding your life to keep peace isn't.
scenarios.relearn: Feeling free to be yourself and owning mistakes are healthy signs.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a green sign, or a red one?

items.text: They guilt you out of plans

scenarios.relearn: Respecting your no and celebrating your wins is green; guilt and competing with you is red.

scenarios.hook: You realise you've slowly stopped seeing your friends since dating someone.

options.text: Reconnect; a healthy relationship leaves room for them
options.consequence: You restore your wider life.

options.text: Let it go; you have your partner now
options.consequence: Losing your friends is a warning sign; a healthy bond leaves room for them.

scenarios.debrief: Keeping your friendships alive is both healthy and a quiet safeguard.
scenarios.relearn: Keep your friendships; a healthy relationship leaves room for them.

scenarios.hook: "You should settle for less to keep someone."
scenarios.relearn: You deserve respect, trust, equality, honesty and space; don't settle below that.

myth.un: You should settle for less to keep someone.
myth.re: You deserve respect, trust, equality, honesty and space; don't settle below that.
myth.why: Settling for less invites being treated as less.

scenarios.hook: Sort: equality, or a power imbalance?
scenarios.relearn: Both opinions counting and sharing is equality; one controlling money or always winning is imbalance.

scenarios.hook: You're not sure if what you have is healthy; it's hard to tell from inside.

options.text: Check it against the markers and trusted friends
options.consequence: You get an honest read.

options.text: Just hope it's fine
options.consequence: Checking against the healthy markers, and trusted friends, gives an honest read.

scenarios.debrief: Measuring against clear markers, and people who know you, beats guessing from inside it.
scenarios.relearn: Check a relationship against the markers and trusted friends.

scenarios.hook: Match the healthy ingredient to what it looks like.
scenarios.relearn: Respect, trust and independence each show up in concrete, daily ways.

scenarios.hook: "A good relationship has no conflict."

myth.un: A good relationship has no conflict.
myth.re: Conflict is normal; how you handle and repair it is what matters.

scenarios.relearn: Conflict is normal; how you handle and repair it is what matters.

scenarios.hook: "If we fight, we're doomed."

myth.re: Fighting fair and repairing is healthy; it's contempt, not conflict, that predicts breakdown.
myth.why: How you fight matters more than whether you fight.

scenarios.relearn: Fighting fair and repairing is healthy; contempt, not conflict, predicts breakdown.

scenarios.hook: Sort: fair fighting, or a relationship-wrecker?
scenarios.relearn: Sticking to the issue and 'I' statements is fair; contempt and stonewalling wreck.

scenarios.hook: "Winning the argument is the point."

myth.un: Winning the argument is the point.
myth.re: The point is understanding each other and repairing, not scoring a win.
myth.why: A 'win' that hurts your partner loses the relationship.

scenarios.relearn: The point of a disagreement is understanding and repair, not winning.

scenarios.hook: Your partner did something that hurt you, and you want to raise it well.
scenarios.setup: Lead with how you felt, not an attack. Say:

yourLine.text: "I felt hurt when that happened. Can we talk about it?"

scenarios.relearn: Raise a hurt with an 'I felt...' opener, not a 'you always' attack.

scenarios.hook: Spot the most corrosive pattern.
scenarios.why: Contempt, sarcasm, mockery, eye-rolling, is the single most damaging pattern; a calm, specific complaint isn't.
scenarios.relearn: Contempt is the single most corrosive pattern in conflict.

scenarios.hook: Mid-argument, you're too flooded to think straight.

options.text: Ask for a short break, then come back to it
options.consequence: You self-soothe and avoid saying something cruel.

options.text: Push on and let it explode
options.consequence: A short break to calm down, then returning, beats exploding; that's not stonewalling if you come back.

scenarios.debrief: Taking a brief, agreed break to calm down, then returning, is healthy, the antidote to both flooding and stonewalling.
scenarios.relearn: When flooded, take a short break and return; don't explode or vanish.

scenarios.hook: You realise you were in the wrong in a fight.
scenarios.setup: A real apology owns it. Say:

yourLine.text: "I was wrong, I'm sorry, and here's what I'll do differently."

scenarios.relearn: A real apology owns your part and names what you'll change.

scenarios.hook: Sort: an antidote to a wrecker, or the wrecker itself?
scenarios.relearn: Taking responsibility and showing appreciation are antidotes; defensiveness and character attacks are wreckers.

scenarios.hook: Your partner raises a complaint and your instinct is to defend yourself.

options.text: Listen first and own any part that's fair
options.consequence: You break the defensiveness loop.

options.text: Immediately list why it's actually their fault
options.consequence: Listening and owning your part beats instant defensiveness, which only escalates.

scenarios.debrief: Defensiveness escalates; listening and taking responsibility de-escalates and repairs.
scenarios.relearn: Listen and own your part instead of getting defensive.

scenarios.hook: "Bringing up every past grievance helps you win."

myth.un: Bringing up every past grievance helps you win.
myth.re: Fair fighting stays on one issue; kitchen-sinking everything just wounds.
myth.why: Piling on the past buries the actual problem.

scenarios.relearn: Fight fair by staying on one issue, not dredging up everything.

scenarios.hook: After a fight, things feel cold and unresolved.

options.text: Make a repair attempt: a kind word, a check-in
options.consequence: You reconnect and close the rupture.

options.text: Let it fester to make a point
options.consequence: A small repair attempt, a kind word or check-in, reconnects; festering only widens the gap.

scenarios.debrief: Repair attempts after conflict are what keep healthy couples close.
scenarios.relearn: Make a repair attempt after a fight; don't let it fester.

scenarios.hook: After a small fight, you want to reconnect rather than stay cold.
scenarios.relearn: Initiating repair kindly reconnects after a fight.

yourLine.text: "I didn't like how we just spoke, can we try that again, kinder?"
Give them the silent treatment to make a point

scenarios.hook: Your partner is stonewalling, gone silent and shut down.
scenarios.setup: Offer a way back, not pressure. Say:

yourLine.text: "Let's take a breather and talk in an hour when we're calmer?"
"Answer me right now or it's over."

scenarios.relearn: Offer a calm break and a time to return rather than pressuring a shut-down partner.

scenarios.hook: Sort: helps a relationship recover from conflict, or harms it?
scenarios.relearn: Apology and naming feelings help recovery; silent treatment and leave-threats harm.

scenarios.hook: Sam: handling conflict well might be the single most useful relationship skill there is. Worth building?
scenarios.affirm: Couples who repair well last; this is a skill worth building for life.
scenarios.relearn: Handling conflict and repairing well is the key relationship skill.

scenarios.hook: "Jealousy means they really love you."

myth.un: Jealousy means they really love you.
myth.re: Jealousy and possessiveness are about control, not love.

scenarios.relearn: Jealousy and possessiveness are about control, not love.

scenarios.hook: "They check my phone and location because they care."

myth.un: They check my phone and location because they care.
myth.re: Monitoring 'for transparency' is control; healthy transparency is voluntary, not demanded.

scenarios.relearn: Monitoring your phone or location 'for transparency' is control, not care.

scenarios.hook: "They're just protective; that's why they don't like my friends."

myth.un: They're just protective about my friends.
myth.re: Cutting you off from friends and family is isolation, a control tactic, not protection.
myth.why: Isolation makes you easier to control.

scenarios.relearn: Cutting you off from friends and family is isolation, not protection.

scenarios.hook: Spot the gaslighting.
scenarios.why: Denying your reality and calling you 'too sensitive' is gaslighting; acknowledging your feelings isn't.
scenarios.relearn: Denying your reality or calling you 'too sensitive' is gaslighting.

scenarios.hook: "Real love means losing yourself in each other."

myth.un: Real love means losing yourself in each other.
myth.re: Healthy love keeps your independence, friends and identity intact.
myth.why: Losing yourself is a warning sign, not romance.

scenarios.relearn: Healthy love keeps your independence, friends and identity intact.

scenarios.hook: Spot coercive control.

scene.text: Controlling what you wear and who you see
Controlling your money 'for your own good'

scenarios.why: Dictating your clothes, contacts or money is coercive control; ordinary interest isn't.
scenarios.relearn: Dictating your clothes, contacts or money is coercive control.

scenarios.hook: Sort: love, or control dressed as love?

items.text: Trusting you with your own choices

scenarios.relearn: Trusting your choices and your friendships is love; demanding passwords and sulking is control.

scenarios.hook: "If I just love them harder, they'll stop controlling me."

myth.un: If I love them harder, they'll stop controlling me.
myth.re: You can't love someone out of controlling or abusing you; that isn't yours to fix.
myth.why: The control is their choice, not your failing.

scenarios.relearn: You can't love someone out of controlling you; it isn't yours to fix.

scenarios.hook: Spot the red flag behind the romantic-sounding line.

scene.text: "I can't live without you" used to guilt you
"If you leave, I'll do something drastic"

scenarios.why: Guilt and threats dressed as devotion are control; genuine warmth isn't.
scenarios.relearn: Guilt and threats dressed as devotion are control, not romance.

scenarios.hook: "They only get angry because they love me so much."

myth.un: They only get angry because they love me so much.
myth.re: Intensity and anger aren't proof of love; respect and safety are.
myth.why: Love isn't measured in jealousy or rage.

scenarios.relearn: Anger and intensity aren't proof of love; respect and safety are.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a healthy boundary, or controlling behaviour?

items.text: "I'm not comfortable with that, let's talk"

scenarios.relearn: Naming your own comfort and needs is a boundary; dictating their clothes or contacts is control.

scenarios.hook: You catch yourself making excuses for a partner's controlling behaviour.

options.text: Name it honestly to yourself; control isn't love
options.consequence: You stop minimising the red flag.

options.text: Keep explaining it away
options.consequence: Naming control honestly, instead of excusing it, is the first step to safety.

scenarios.debrief: Recognising and naming control, rather than excusing it, is how you start to get clear and safe.
scenarios.relearn: Name controlling behaviour honestly instead of excusing it.

scenarios.hook: Spot the early warning sign.

scene.text: Moving very fast and 'you're my everything'
Getting to know each other slowly

scenarios.why: Rushing intimacy and put-down 'jokes' are early control signs; a slow, respectful start isn't.
scenarios.relearn: Rushing intensity and put-down 'jokes' are early control warning signs.

scenarios.hook: Sort: expands your world, or shrinks it?

items.text: Makes you account for every hour

scenarios.relearn: Love expands your world; control slowly shrinks it.

scenarios.hook: A friend's partner shows clear signs of coercive control.

options.text: Stay connected, name it gently, don't judge them
options.consequence: You keep a lifeline open without pushing them away.

options.text: Tell them to just dump the loser and back off if they don't
options.consequence: Staying connected and non-judgmental keeps a lifeline; ultimatums can isolate them further.

scenarios.debrief: For someone in a controlling relationship, a steady, non-judgmental friend is a vital lifeline.
scenarios.relearn: Stay a steady, non-judgmental lifeline for a friend facing control.

scenarios.hook: Sam: love expands your world; control shrinks it. A line you can hold onto?
scenarios.affirm: That one line, love expands, control shrinks, can keep you clear for life.
scenarios.relearn: Love expands your world; control shrinks it.

scenarios.hook: "Leaving means I failed at the relationship."

myth.re: Leaving an unhealthy or unsafe relationship is brave and valid, not a failure.
myth.why: Choosing your safety and wellbeing is strength.

scenarios.relearn: Leaving an unhealthy or unsafe relationship is brave and valid, not a failure.

scenarios.hook: Sam: if a relationship is hurting or controlling you, none of it is your fault. Hear that?
scenarios.affirm: Abuse and control are never the target's fault; the responsibility is the person doing it.
scenarios.relearn: Abuse and control are never the target's fault.

scenarios.hook: You've decided to leave a controlling relationship and you're a little scared.

options.text: Make a quiet plan: tell someone, a safe place, key documents
options.consequence: You set up a safer exit.

options.text: Announce it in the heat of a fight
options.consequence: Because abuse can escalate at leaving, a quiet plan, told someone, safe place, documents, is safer than a heated announcement.

scenarios.debrief: Abuse can escalate around leaving, so a plan, a trusted person, a safe place, important documents and a helpline, matters.
scenarios.relearn: Leave with a plan: tell someone, a safe place, key documents, a helpline.

scenarios.hook: You need to tell a trusted person you're planning to leave and want support.

yourLine.text: "I'm planning to leave and I'm a bit scared, can you help me stay safe?"
Tell no one and handle it alone

scenarios.relearn: Tell a trusted person and ask for help to leave safely; you don't have to do it alone.

scenarios.hook: A partner who controls you says they'll change if you stay, again.

options.text: Notice the pattern; promises without change aren't safety
options.consequence: You don't get pulled back by another promise.

options.text: Believe it and stay one more time
options.consequence: Repeated promises without real change are part of the cycle; trust the pattern, not the promise.

scenarios.debrief: Cycles of promise-and-repeat are common in controlling relationships; the pattern tells the truth.
scenarios.relearn: Promises without real change aren't safety; trust the pattern.

scenarios.hook: Sam: you deserve to feel safe and free in love, fully. Believe that for yourself?
scenarios.affirm: You absolutely deserve to feel safe, respected and free; never settle below that.
scenarios.relearn: You deserve to feel safe, respected and free in a relationship.

scenarios.hook: Since leaving, your ex keeps contacting and pressuring you to come back.

options.text: Go no-contact and tell someone; block if needed
options.consequence: You protect your space and safety.

options.text: Keep replying to keep the peace
options.consequence: No-contact and telling someone protects you; persistent pressure after leaving is a reason to get support.

scenarios.debrief: No-contact and support after leaving protect you; persistent pressure is itself a warning to take seriously.
scenarios.relearn: After leaving, go no-contact, tell someone, and block if needed.

scenarios.hook: A friend confides their partner is controlling and frightening them.

yourLine.text: "I believe you, it's not your fault, and I'm here. Want to make a safe plan together?"

scenarios.relearn: Believe a friend, tell them it's not their fault, and offer to plan safety together.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a safer-leaving step, or a risk?

items.text: Threatening them back in a fight
Knowing a helpline and safe place

scenarios.relearn: Confiding in someone and knowing a helpline and safe place is safer; confronting alone is a risk.

scenarios.hook: Sam: walking away from what's hurting you is one of the bravest things a person does. Own that?
scenarios.affirm: Leaving takes real courage; if you do it, you're brave, not a failure.
scenarios.relearn: Walking away from what's hurting you is brave, not a failure.

scenarios.hook: You feel ashamed that you 'let it get this far'.

options.text: Drop the shame; control is engineered to trap people
options.consequence: You release self-blame and move forward.

options.text: Keep blaming yourself
options.consequence: Control is designed to trap anyone; the shame belongs to the controller, not you.

scenarios.debrief: Coercive control traps capable people by design; staying as long as you did is not a personal failing.
scenarios.relearn: Control traps people by design; the shame isn't yours.

scenarios.hook: You're out, but part of you misses even the bad relationship.

options.text: Accept that's normal, lean on support, stay out
options.consequence: You ride the pull without going back.

options.text: Take it as a sign you should return

scenarios.hook: Sam: leaving isn't the end of your story, it's the start of a safer one. Hold onto that?

scenarios.relearn: Leaving is the start of a safer story, not the end.

scenarios.hook: Sam: heartbreak is real grief, and it's survivable. Does naming it that way help?
